Chapter 7: The Art World Reckons
For years, the Sackler name was like a golden ticket in the art world. Museums and galleries would line up for their donations, hoping to land another new wing or a blockbuster exhibition, all thanks to the family’s well-known generosity.
But as the opioid crisis deepened, and the link to OxyContin became impossible to ignore, something started to change. The art world found itself at a crossroads.
At first, it was just a quiet hesitation—a curator at a major museum pausing before announcing a new Sackler-funded exhibit. She remembered the protests outside, the angry letters from families who’d lost loved ones to addiction.
She couldn’t help but wonder: was all this money really worth the pain it caused?
Then, artists started to find their voices. One sculptor, whose work was set to be displayed in a Sackler gallery, made a tough call—she pulled her piece in protest. No big speech, just a short note explaining she couldn’t support something tied to so much suffering.
And that quiet act? It inspired others to take a stand. Protests grew louder. Pressure on museums kept building.
Some institutions tried to push back. They argued, “We’ve already spent the money,” or, “Art and donors should be separate.” But the tide was turning fast.
One by one, museums began announcing they’d no longer accept Sackler donations. Some even took the family’s name off their walls—a strong, symbolic move that sent shockwaves through the world of philanthropy.
For the Sacklers, this was a different kind of loss. Their name, once a symbol of culture and generosity, had become something to hide.
The art world, which had always welcomed them, was now turning away.
And what became clear, in the end, is that reputation—once it’s lost—is almost impossible to win back. The true cost of their fortune wasn’t just measured in dollars anymore, but in the loss of respect, and a sense of belonging.
